challenges.name: read-explain-analyze-quiz
challenges.title: Read the plan: loops and costs
challenges.description: Two plans from the CodeDev database: the slow course progress query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and an activity feed query with plain EXPLAIN. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

questions.question:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) of the course progress query for course 42:

Sort  (cost=1004.71..1005.01 rows=120 width=40) (actual time=1213.054..1214.871 rows=18204 loops=1)
  Sort Key: lp.completed_at DESC
  Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 1985kB
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.99..1000.57 rows=120 width=40) (actual time=0.092..1209.330 rows=18204 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using enrollments_course_id_idx on enrollments e  (cost=0.43..412.10 rows=120 width=16) (actual time=0.031..21.402 rows=18204 loops=1)
              Index Cond: (course_id = 42)
              Filter: (status = 'active'::text)
              Rows Removed by Filter: 611
        ->  Index Scan using lesson_progress_user_id_course_id_idx on lesson_progress lp  (cost=0.56..4.89 rows=1 width=32) (actual time=0.058..0.064 rows=1 loops=18204)
              Index Cond: ((user_id = e.user_id) AND (course_id = 42))
Planning Time: 0.412 ms
Execution Time: 1216.022 ms

Statement: "About 1,165 ms of the 1,216 ms execution is spent inside the Index Scan on lesson_progress, even though its actual time reads only 0.064 ms."
questions.explanation: True. The actual time of a node is the average for one execution, and loops=18204 says the inner side of the Nested Loop ran 18,204 times, once per enrollment row. Its total time is 0.064 ms x 18,204 = 1,165 ms. The Nested Loop's own work is then 1,209.330 - 21.402 - 1,165.056 = about 23 ms and the Sort adds about 5.5 ms on top of its child, so the Sort at the top is not the problem even though it shows the largest number. The common misconception is to read actual time as a total and to blame the first node whose time is large: always multiply by loops and subtract the children before you decide where the time goes.

questions.question:
EXPLAIN (without ANALYZE) of the activity feed query:

EXPLAIN SELECT id, user_id, kind, created_at
FROM activity_log
WHERE kind = 'quiz_submitted'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

Limit  (cost=0.56..41.93 rows=50 width=36)
  ->  Index Scan Backward using activity_log_created_at_idx on activity_log  (cost=0.56..2391755.12 rows=2890500 width=36)
        Filter: (kind = 'quiz_submitted'::text)

Statement: "The planner predicts that this query will run for about 42 ms."
questions.explanation: False. Costs are in the planner's own units, scaled so that reading one page sequentially costs seq_page_cost = 1.0; they are not milliseconds and plain EXPLAIN never measures or predicts time. 41.93 means the planner expects to stop after about 50/2,890,500 of the index scan's total cost of 2,391,755 units, because LIMIT ends the scan early. Costs are for comparing alternative plans of the same query; to know how long it runs you need EXPLAIN ANALYZE (which really executes it) or the timings in pg_stat_statements. The misconception is reading cost as a duration, then being surprised when a plan with a small cost runs for seconds because the 50 matching rows are not near the end of the index.

challenges.name: find-the-hottest-plan-node
challenges.title: Find the hottest node in an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan
challenges.description:
The CodeDev slow-query dashboard stores the EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) output of every query that auto_explain logs. On-call developers keep blaming the top node of a plan because it shows the largest actual time. Write analyze_plan(explain) so the dashboard can show where the time really goes and which estimates were wrong.

Input (stdin, one test case): the JSON that PostgreSQL prints for EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON) - a list with one object holding "Plan", "Planning Time" and "Execution Time". Each plan node has "Node Type", optionally "Relation Name", "Plan Rows" (the planner's estimate per execution), "Actual Total Time" (ms, average per execution), "Actual Rows" (average per execution), "Actual Loops" (how many times the node ran) and, when it has children, "Plans". Every entry of "Plans" is a child, whatever its "Parent Relationship" (Outer, Inner, Member, InitPlan, SubPlan). The fixtures have no parallel workers.

Output: {"execution_ms": <Execution Time>, "hottest": <id>, "nodes": [...]}
- Number the nodes 1, 2, 3 ... depth-first: a node, then its "Plans" in order. One dict per node in that order: {"id", "node": Node Type, "relation": Relation Name or null, "loops": Actual Loops, "self_ms", "rows", "rows_ratio"}.
- inclusive time = Actual Total Time x Actual Loops; self_ms = inclusive time of the node - sum of the inclusive times of its children, rounded to 3 decimals and never below 0 (per-loop times are rounded averages, so the difference can come out a little negative).
- rows = Actual Rows x Actual Loops.
- rows_ratio = (Actual Rows x Actual Loops) / (Plan Rows x Actual Loops), rounded to 2 decimals (above 1: the planner underestimated); null when the node never ran (Actual Loops = 0, shown as "never executed" in the text format).
- hottest = id of the node with the largest self_ms; the smallest id wins a tie.
- A plan without actual times (plain EXPLAIN, no ANALYZE) prints {"error": "no actual times: run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, FORMAT JSON)"}.

Example: a Sort (Actual Total Time 4.630, 1 loop) over a Seq Scan on courses (3.912, 1 loop, 1240 actual rows, 1250 planned) gives the Sort self_ms 0.718, the Seq Scan self_ms 3.912 and rows_ratio 0.99, and hottest 2. The code runner has no PostgreSQL: this is plain Python over JSON.
hints: An inner Index Scan shows actual time 0.064 ms and loops 18204. How many milliseconds did the query really spend in it, and how much of its parent's time is then left for the parent itself?

Look at the two numbers you multiply for every node - for the node itself and for each of its children - and at which children you subtract: a SubPlan or an InitPlan sits in "Plans" next to Outer and Inner. Then check a node with "Actual Loops": 0 before you divide by anything.

A similar walk on a different plan: a Hash Join (Actual Total Time 50.0, loops 1) has a Seq Scan child (30.0, loops 1) and a Hash child (8.0, loops 1), and the Hash has a Seq Scan child (7.9, loops 1). Inclusive times are 50.0, 30.0, 8.0 and 7.9; self times are 50.0 - 30.0 - 8.0 = 12.0 for the join, 30.0, 8.0 - 7.9 = 0.1 for the Hash and 7.9. A recursive function that returns nothing and appends one dict per node to a shared list keeps the depth-first order for free.

Hash join under an aggregate; rounding noise never gives a negative self time
InitPlan and SubPlan children: the correlated subquery is the hottest node
Zero rows and a never-executed inner node (Actual Loops = 0)
Large plan: Append over 160 partitions, one slow partition
